name: Money Laundering Networks
title: Money Laundering Networks
answer: This page covers the use of artificial intelligence to identify, map, and disrupt money laundering networks. It addresses the full laundering cycle, including placement, layering, and integration, across fiat payment rails, trade finance, real estate, and virtual assets. The focus is on network-level detection rather than single transaction screening, because launderers typically move value through chains of accounts, shell companies, and intermediaries. Readers will find material on typologies such as trade-based laundering, smurfing, and shell company layering, as well as the data and models used to expose them.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: This page covers the use of artificial intelligence to identify, map, and disrupt money laundering networks. It addresses the full laundering cycle, including placement, layering, and integration, across fiat payment rails, trade finance, real estate, and virtual assets. The focus is on network-level detection rather than single transaction screening, because launderers typically move value through chains of accounts, shell companies, and intermediaries. Readers will find material on typologies such as trade-based laundering, smurfing, and shell company layering, as well as the data and models used to expose them.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Money laundering network detection runs on a mix of internal transaction systems, external watchlists, corporate registries, and blockchain ledgers. The core technical substrate is usually a graph database or graph processing engine, which stores accounts, entities, and transactions as nodes and edges so that hidden relationships can be queried at scale. Batch and streaming pipelines feed these graphs from core banking, payment, and trade platforms, while entity resolution tools link records that refer to the same person or company across sources. Compute requirements are moderate for rule-based screening but rise sharply for graph neural networks and large-scale link prediction, often calling for GPU or distributed processing.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work typically begins with entity resolution and feature engineering, turning raw transactions and counterparty records into a connected graph. Analysts and models then look for structural patterns associated with laundering, such as cycles, rapid value transfer through intermediaries, or clusters of shell companies with no obvious economic purpose. Supervised models are trained on historical suspicious activity reports and confirmed cases, while unsupervised methods like anomaly detection and community detection surface unusual subnetworks without labeled examples. Graph neural networks and link prediction are increasingly used to infer missing relationships, such as undisclosed beneficial ownership or coordinated behavior across seemingly unrelated accounts.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Money laundering network models operate under strict data protection, bank secrecy, and anti-money laundering rules, and their outputs can trigger regulatory filings or freeze assets. Key risks include false positives that burden innocent customers, biased risk scoring against certain geographies or business types, and the difficulty of explaining why a graph model flagged a particular network. Provenance matters because suspicious activity reports and law enforcement referrals require a clear chain from source data to model output, and cross-border data sharing is often limited by privacy and blocking statutes. Model risk management, human review, and audit trails are standard controls, but they do not remove the need for careful handling of personal and commercially sensitive information.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward real-time network detection, where transaction graphs are updated continuously and alerts are raised as laundering structures form rather than after the fact. Federated learning and privacy-preserving techniques may allow banks to compare patterns without sharing raw customer data, while generative models are being explored to create synthetic laundering networks for training and stress testing. Explainable graph models and tighter links to beneficial ownership registries are likely to improve both detection and regulatory acceptance. Over time, the same network methods are expected to extend further into trade finance, decentralized finance, and cross-border payment corridors where laundering activity is hardest to trace.
